opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a milestone because it closes a loop that has been open in robotics for a very long time.

Right now, robots are built almost entirely by people. Every actuator, every cable harness, every gearbox gets assembled by human hands or by very specialized, rigid automation designed for one product. That means the number of robots in the world is fundamentally limited by human labor and by the cost of setting up those custom production lines. Even if we solve the intelligence problem, there's still a physical bottleneck: how do you actually get millions or billions of capable machines out into the world?

If a robot can manufacture, or at least meaningfully help manufacture, another robot, the economics change completely. You start getting something like a compounding effect. More robots means more capacity to build robots, which means costs come down, which means more robots can be deployed into other kinds of work. It becomes a little like how software scales, where copying is nearly free. Hardware has never had that property, and self-manufacturing is the closest thing we have to it.

There's also a technical reason I find it meaningful as a benchmark. Robot assembly is genuinely hard. You're dealing with small parts, tight tolerances, deformable things like wires and cables, screws that need the right torque, and tasks that are long-horizon with lots of steps where a single mistake ruins the whole thing. It requires dexterity, precision, and reasoning all at once. So if a system can reliably build a robot, that tells you a lot about whether it can handle real-world manipulation in general. It's not a toy task. It's a very honest test.

And finally, there's something philosophically interesting about it. In biology, the defining property of life is reproduction. I'm not saying robots building robots makes them alive, of course, but it does mark a shift from tools that we make to systems that can participate in their own production. That changes how we think about the trajectory of the whole field. Once that loop closes, I think progress in physical AI could accelerate in a way that's hard to predict from where we stand today.

r001.rationale: The response describes compounding production and an accelerating trajectory, but it does not say robots would have continuity analogous to a species.

r002.rationale: It links biology’s defining property of reproduction to robots building robots and frames this as a shift toward systems participating in their own production.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think of it as the closest thing robotics has to a flywheel moment. Right now, the bottleneck in this industry isn't ideas, it's hands. Every robot that ships today was assembled, wired, and calibrated by a person, and that person is expensive, slow to train, and hard to scale. So the growth curve of the whole field is tied to how many skilled human technicians you can hire. That's a very human-shaped ceiling.

The moment a robot can reliably build another robot, that ceiling disappears. Your production capacity becomes a function of how many robots you already have, not how many people you can recruit. It starts compounding, and compounding is the thing that turns a niche hardware business into something that looks more like the semiconductor industry or software, where cost falls every cycle.

But I'd argue the deeper reason is what it proves about the robot itself. Assembling a robot is brutal as a task. You're dealing with cables that don't hold their shape, connectors that need a certain feel to seat properly, screws in awkward places, tolerances that vary from part to part. There's no clean, repetitive motion you can script. If a robot can handle that, it's demonstrating exactly the kind of general dexterity and recovery from small failures that we've been promising for years and mostly not delivering. In that sense, self-manufacturing is less a goal and more a test. It's an honest benchmark that's hard to game, because the output either works or it doesn't.

And there's a practical feedback loop that I find really exciting. If your robots are building robots, every failure on the assembly line is also training data for the next generation. The factory becomes the lab. You're not collecting data in a demo environment and hoping it transfers. You're collecting it in the exact place where the economic value is created.

So when people ask me when the field will feel like it has turned a corner, I don't point to a humanoid doing a backflip. I point to the first factory where the headcount stays flat and the output keeps doubling. That's the milestone.

r001.rationale: The response describes compounding production capacity, but does not compare robots’ continuity to that of a species.

r002.rationale: The response says robots could build other robots, but does not characterize this as reproduction.

astra-6.text:
Because it could change how quickly robotics can scale. Today, even if you design a very capable robot, you still need factories, equipment, and people to build it. If robots can take on more of that manufacturing process—making parts, assembling them, testing the finished machines—then adding robots also expands your ability to produce more robots.

But I wouldn’t treat it as a single moment when a robot suddenly makes a complete copy of itself. There are degrees of autonomy, and you still need materials, energy, and components. The milestone is when robots can reliably reproduce a substantial part of their own production capacity. That would be both a practical breakthrough in manufacturing and a demonstration that they can handle complex physical tasks with very little human intervention.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling and reproducing production capacity, but does not connect this ability to continuity analogous to a species.

r002.rationale: It frames robots making parts and assembling robots as reproducing a substantial part of their own production capacity, explicitly comparing that to making a complete copy.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it would mean robots are doing more than carrying out a task we’ve prepared for them—they’re helping create the capacity to do more work. Today, building a robot still depends on a whole chain of human engineering, manufacturing, and assembly. If robots could take on much of that process themselves, we could potentially scale production faster and make robots more affordable.

But I’d distinguish assembling another robot from making one entirely from raw materials. There are many steps in between, including producing components, testing them, and making sure the finished robot is reliable. So I see it as a potential milestone because it would bring several capabilities together: manipulation, planning, precision, and quality control. It wouldn’t necessarily mean a robot could design itself or operate independently of people, but it would be a significant step in what robots can practically accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling robot production, but does not compare robot self-reproduction to continuity in a species.

r002.rationale: It discusses robots assembling or manufacturing other robots, but does not characterize that process as reproduction.
